questions.question_text: Which of the following modes of psychotherapy has established evidence in HIV-associated depression?
questions.explanation:
Interpersonal psychotherapy may be particularly bene�cial for HIV patients with depressive symptoms. Markowitz and colleagues enrolled
65 HIV-infected men and 4 women (53% with major depression; 32% with AIDS) in a 16-week trial comparing interpersonal psychotherapy
(IPT), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), supportive therapy with imipramine (SWI), and supportive therapy alone (SP). IPT and SWI were
superior to SP and CBT in ameliorating depressive symptoms and improving Karnofsky performance score (a measure of physical function).
This study suggested that combining psychotherapy with medication may be the optimal approach to treating depression in HIV.

Role reversal is a technique typical to psychodrama and is considered as the single most e�ective instrument in therapeutic role-playing. It

Infanticide is the intentional killing of infants and neonaticide is the killing within 24 hours of birth. Infanticide rates are very low in the West
(1 in 3000 –5000 children of all ages (Putkonen et al. BMC Psychiatry 2009; 9:74) and 2.1 per 100 000 newborns per year (Herman-Giddenset
et al. JAMA 2003; 289:1425 –9)). The risk factors for infanticide include (1) domestic violence and a history of childhood maltreatment in the

pregnancies in young women. Women who commit infanticide are often young, frequently fail to report symptoms of pregnancy and do not
attend antenatal clinics.

Background: Evidence suggests that there is an association between antipsychotic drugs and new-onset diabetes, but little is known about
the risk of hyperglycaemia among persons with pre-existing diabetes.

with an antipsychotic drug from April 1, 2002, to March 31, 2006, were followed up from treatment start until March 31, 2007. The cohort

patients hospitalized (emergency department visit or hospital admissions) for hyperglycaemia. Each case was matched with up to 10
controls for age, sex, year of cohort entry and duration of follow-up. The authors compared the likelihood of hyperglycaemia among current
users of atypical and typical antipsychotic agents with that among remote antipsychotic users (discontinued >180 days), based on
prescriptions closest to the event date.
Results: Of 13 817 patients studied, 1515 (11.0%) were hospitalized for hyperglycaemia. Current antipsychotic treatment was associated with
a higher risk of hyperglycaemia compared with remote antipsychotic use in all diabetes treatment groups (overall adjusted rate ratio, 1.50;
95% con�dence interval, 1.29-1.74). The risk was increased among patients who were treated with atypical and typical antipsychotic agents
and was extremely high among patients who were just starting treatment (only 1 prescription before event).
Conclusions: Among older patients with diabetes, the initiation of treatment with antipsychotic drugs was associated with a signi�cantly
increased risk of hospitalization for hyperglycaemia (P < .001). The risk was particularly high during the initial course of treatment and was
increased with the use of all antipsychotic agents. Ref: Lipscombe et al., Arch Intern Med. 2009;169(14):1282-1289

Total alcohol consumption is expressed by the 'per capita consumption'�gure for persons over the age of 15. It is the average amount of
pure alcohol (in litres) consumed in one year. It is calculated from the total amount of pure alcohol consumed in one year by the whole
population (including children and abstainers), divided by the number of adults (in this case persons over the age of 15). The prevalence of
alcohol related problems in a community is linked to Per capita alcohol consumption

questions.question_text: With regard to the epidemiology of addiction disorders in the UK, which of the following holds true?

options.text: 10% of cannabis users start using the drug below the age of 24
Cocaine is the most prevalent abused substance in the UK
1% of the adult population smoke cannabis regularly
2% of all school children used cannabis in the last year.
About 40% of users are below the age of 24

correct_answer.text: About 40% of users are below the age of 24

questions.explanation:
Men (38%) are more than twice as likely to have any alcohol use disorder as women (16%). One in ten of 16 - 24 year olds used hard drugs in
the last month. Cocaine is used by one and three quarter million young adults, but is less common than cannabis in the UK. 10% of the adult
population smoke cannabis regularly. The highest numbers of drug users are amongst young adults under 25. 45% have used drugs at some
point. Half of all cannabis users are under 24. 12% of all school children used cannabis in the last year. From Addicted Britain: State of the
Nation report 2006.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with regard to the epidemiology of alcohol use?

options.text: A large health burden is attributable to moderate drinkers
Conclusive evidence suggests light drinking is bene�cial to health
There is a trend of reducing home drinking
Most drinkers in the population are heavy users of alcohol

correct_answer.text: A large health burden is attributable to moderate drinkers

questions.explanation:
Chronic heavy drinking (as with alcohol dependency) tends to cause longer-term health problems, whilst binge drinking (de�ned as
consuming more than twice the daily recommended levels in one session) is more likely to increase the risk of acute health e�ects. Because
moderate drinkers make up >50% of the alcohol users in the population, a large proportion of public health burden stems from this group.
70% of admissions to accident and emergency departments at peak times are alcohol-related. Home measures are often larger than pub
measures - and as prices in licensed premises increase, and o�-licence prices decrease, more people are drinking at home and therefore
potentially drinking a lot more than they think. (from www.adph.org.uk)

questions.question_text:
Mrs Dundheim comes to see you in clinic, accompanied by her adult daughter. You notice that there is some disturbance in her movements.
Her daughter tells you that her mother's sister had Parkinson's Disease, and she's worried her mother might also have it. Which of the
following physical signs is most indicative of Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation:
A pill-rolling tremor, occurring at rest, is suggestive of Parkinson's disease, alongside bradykinesia, rigidity (both sides of the body, may start
as unilateral rigidity), and mask-like facial appearance due to reduced facial expressions.

questions.question_text:
The mental health liaison nurse has assessed a person presenting with suicidal ideas in the emergency department and asks you conduct a
review. She is concerned that this person is at high risk. You look over her notes. What description of the patient is linked with the highest
risk of suicide?

options.text: 32-year-old woman, married, subject to domestic violence
16-year-old woman, recently split up from boyfriend

questions.explanation:
Middle age, male gender, unemployment, with recent major loss are all signi�cant factors in contributing to the risk of suicide. This is made
even higher by alcohol and/or drug misuse.

questions.question_text:
Ben White is a 22-year-old student who attends A&E complaining of feeling out of touch with his body. He's not been able to sleep all night,
he has stomach cramps, and on observation he's sweating profusely. He is worried it might be related to drug use. Which of the following
clinical states in the best explanation?
questions.explanation: These are typical features of withdrawal from opioids, also accompanied by piloerection, muscle spasms, and tremors.

questions.question_text:
You are due to visit a 85 year old woman who lives alone, and who has for some months been complaining about her neighbour spying on
her, listening to her movements through the walls, tapping on the walls when she's trying to sleep. Which if the following feature is most
likely to be seen in persistent delusional disorder?
questions.explanation:
Persistent delusional disorder is often characterized by life long persistent non-bizarre delusions. The others are more suggestive of a
broader psychotic illness, including schizophrenia.

questions.question_text:
A 40-year-old man has had 5 depressive episodes in the past and every time following treatment of depression he had developed
hypomania. What would you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Antidepressant-induced mania/hypomania has been reported with all major antidepressant classes in a subgroup of about 20-40% of
bipolar patients. Lithium may confer better protection against this outcome when compared with other standard mood stabilizers, although
switch rates have been reported with comparable frequencies on or o� mood stabilizers. Mood switches were less frequent in patients
receiving lithium (15%) than in patients not treated with lithium (44%) in a small naturalistic study. Risk factors for antidepressant induced
switch includes (i) previous antidepressant-induced manias, (ii) a bipolar family history, and (iii) exposure to multiple antidepressant trials
and (iv) initial illness beginning in adolescence or young adulthood. Henry C, Sorbara F, Lacoste J, Gindre C, Leboyer M. Antidepressant-
induced mania in bipolar patients: identi�cation of risk factors. J Clin Psychiatry 2001 Apr;62(4):249-55

questions.question_text: Which of the following has good evidence as an add-on therapy in partial responders with depression taking antidepressants?
questions.explanation: The role of lithium as an augmenting agent is well established.

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychotropic medication is contraindicated during breastfeeding?
questions.explanation:
Lithium is contraindicated during breast-feeding ( Kohen, 2005) .However, "the use of lithium during breast feeding varies between absolute
contraindication to mother's informed choice" (Maudsley Guidelines, 2007).Lithium serum concentration and CBC should be monitored for
infants exposed to lithium. 40- 50% of maternal serum level is excreted in breast milk. Infant serum level can rise up to 200% of maternal
serum concentration (range 5%-200%). Serum level in lithium can be raised due to diminished renal clearance in neonates. Toxicity has been
reported -cyanosis, lethargy, Hypotonia, heart murmur ( these symptoms resolved after stopping the breast feeding)

questions.question_text:
You started a patient severe depression on medications, and she is currently on 225 mg of venlafaxine and 45 mg of Mirtazapine. She has
improved but developed a mixed a�ective state. What will you do?

options.text: Tell patient to take enough rest

questions.explanation:
Lithium has mood stabilizing properties, which are helpful in mixed a�ective states. Lithium will augment the e�ect of anti-depressants. But
as mixed state must be managed in the same way as mania, we must discontinue the antidepressants, atleast the one with higher likelihood
of switch; in this instance Venlafaxine.

questions.question_text: The sudden withdrawal of antiparkinsonian drugs could cause;
questions.explanation:
Levodopa preparations lead in the long term to the development of motor complications characterized by involuntary movements called
dyskinesia and �uctuations in the response to medication. Levodopa doses are maintained as low as possible while maintaining
functionality. A former strategy to reduce motor complications was to withdraw patients from L-DOPA for some time. It is discouraged now
since it can bring dangerous side e�ects such as neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Most people will eventually need levodopa and may
develop residual motor complications Ref: Oxford handbook of medicine

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for puerperal psychosis?
questions.explanation: Lack of social support is a risk factor for postnatal depression but not for puerperal psychosis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common prescribed medication causing secondary mania?
questions.explanation:
L-Dopa and corticosteroids are the most common prescribed medications associated with secondary mania. Anabolic steroids, amantadine,
bromocriptine, isoniazid, zidovudine and ephedrine (stimulant) can also cause secondary mania. In stimulant or other street drugs induced
mania, if the mood state signi�cantly outlasts the drugged state then a diagnosis of bipolar disorder can be made.Evans DL, et al. Secondary
mania: diagnosis and treatment. J Clin Psychiatry. 1995; 56:31-37.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about Korasako�'s syndrome is incorrect?

options.text: Confabulation and apathy are often prominent symptoms in the syndrome.
Korasako�s syndrome is often associated with Wernicke's encephalopathy, which is the associated syndrome of confusion, ataxia, and
Korasako�s syndrome is caused by thiamine de�ciency, most commonly associated with chronic alcohol abuse.
Remote memory tends to be a�ected more than recent memory
Patients with Korasako�s syndrome typically demonstrate a change in personality and these changes appear frontal lobe-like.

correct_answer.text: Remote memory tends to be a�ected more than recent memory

questions.explanation:
Korsako�s syndrome: Korsako�s syndrome is an Amnestic syndrome caused by thiamine de�ciency, most commonly associated with
chronic alcohol abuse. Other conditions such as prolonged starvation, gastric carcinoma, haemodialysis, hyperemesis gravidarum and
gastric plication can also result in thiamine de�ciency. Korsako�s syndrome is often associated with Wernicke's encephalopathy, which is the

degeneration. They tend to display a lack of initiative, diminished spontaneity, apathy and a lack of interest or concern. Recent memory
tends to be a�ected more than is remote memory, but this feature is variable.

questions.question_text: Major depressive disorders are common in infarcts involving which part of the brain?
questions.explanation:
It was thought that left-hemisphere lesions produce more major or minor depression; this has been contested recently. Major depressive
disorders are common in infarcts involving the basal ganglia, especially on the left hemisphere.

questions.question_text:
A known bipolar patient relapses to a manic episode despite being on long-term mood stabiliser treatment with lithium. What will be the
�rst intervention?
questions.explanation: It is sensible to check adequacy of lithium levels before planning other interventions.

questions.question_text:
Jane is a 15-year-old girl currently admitted under the mental health act to an adolescent unit. She is having her �rst episode of mania with
psychotic features, having previously had a history of depression and been prescribed �uoxetine. Which ONE of the following would be
appropriate as a single agent in treatment of Jane's mania?
questions.explanation:
Recommended �rst line treatments for acute mania in children and adolescents include atypical antipsychotics such as aripiprazole,
olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone. Lithium can be used but would not be appropriate for Jane as a monotherapy as she has psychotic
symptoms. Carbamazepine is not recommended. Sodium Valproate has not shown e�cacy in a small RCT for adolescent mania. (Reference:
Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Bipolar illness in children and adolescents. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th
ed. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, pp.364-365).

questions.question_text:
James is a 17-year-old boy who was diagnosed with ADHD at the age of 8. He is seeing you in CAMHS and has asked about the
neurobiological basis of his illness. He is aware the fronto-striatal network is implicated. Which brain region does NOT form part of the
fronto-striatal network?
questions.explanation:
Data from neuroimaging, neuropsychology, neurochemistry and genetics consistently implicate the fronto-striatal network as a major
contributor to the pathophysiology of ADHD. The network involves the lateral prefrontal cortex, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, the
caudate nucleus and putamen. The cerebellum is not part of the network. (Ref: Emond V, Joyal C, Poissant H. Structural and functional
neuroanatomy of attention-de�cit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). L‘encéphale. 2009 Apr;35(2):107-14).

questions.question_text:
Mr Neil Slater is a 16-year-old boy with a diagnosis of autistic spectrum disorder. He attends a special school and is soon to go to college.
What is the likelihood that he would also have a diagnosis of epilepsy?
questions.explanation:
A recent study suggested that 22% of people with an autism spectrum disorder develop epilepsy by the age of 21 years. This is in keeping
with previous studies. (Ref: Bolton PF, Carcani-Rathwell I, Hutton J, Goode S, Howlin P, Rutter M. Epilepsy in autism: features and correlates.
The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2011 Apr;198(4):289-94.)

questions.question_text:
Miss Joan Sta�ord is a 15-year-old girl who has been su�ering from persistent low mood, reduced interest in activities, irritability, poor sleep
and appetite, and diminishing school performance. She has had a trial of CBT which was not e�ective. Her parents are not willing for her to
have any medications. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step for her treatment?
questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines for treatment of depression in children and adolescents' states that if a trial of an initial psychological intervention is
unsuccessful, an alternative, such of CBT, interpersonal therapy or family therapy should be considered. Fluoxetine can also be considered if
the patient or carers are accepting of this. Repeating a therapy that has been ine�ective would not be helpful and counselling is unlikely to
be successful if a formal psychotherapy has not worked. Individual psychotherapy and systemic family therapy are generally o�ered after
two trials of psychotherapy has been unsuccessful.

questions.question_text:
Oliver is a 10-year-old boy who sustained a head injury falling from his skateboard 2 months ago. At the time he lost consciousness for less
than 1 minute and had a GCS of 14 when he was later seen in A&E. He had some vomiting which settled within 24 hours of the injury. You
are now seeing him 2 months later in CAMHS and his mother is wondering if there is a link between the head injury and his current
complaint. Which ONE of the following neuropsychiatric syndromes or symptoms is NOT associated with mild Traumatic Brain Injury (mTBI)
in children?
questions.explanation:
A systematic review found consistent associations between mTBI and ADHD, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety. However the review
did suggest that the lack of pre-injury reports make �rm conclusions di�cult. Mania has not been reported. (Ref: Emery CA, Barlow KM,
Brooks BL, Max JE, Villavicencio-Requis A, Gnanakumar V, Robertson HL, Schneider K, Yeates KO. A systematic review of psychiatric,
psychological, and behavioural outcomes following mild traumatic brain injury in children and adolescents. The Canadian Journal of
Psychiatry. 2016 May;61(5):259-69).

questions.question_text:
Andrew Davies is a 9-year-old boy who has a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. His mother has noticed that sometimes he can
comment on individual aspects of an object but not seem to see it as a ‘whole'. She gives the example of him being able to talk about wheels
on a toy car but not being able to identify its overall shape. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Central coherence theory underlies the central disturbance seen in people with autistic spectrum disorders. It is considered as a speci�c
perceptual-cognitive style. It is loosely described as a limited ability to understand context or to "see the big picture".

questions.question_text:
Jake is a 12-year-old boy with a diagnosis of conduct disorder. He has been assessed to have normal intelligence and does not have ADHD.
His family have completed a course of multi-systemic therapy with a small bene�t. However, he continues to initiate �ghts at school, has
tortured the family dog and recently lit a �re in a rubbish bin outside his home. Which ONE of the following medications would be indicated?
questions.explanation:
Risperidone is licensed for the short-term management of severely aggressive behaviour in young people with conduct disorder who have
not responded to psychosocial interventions. Quetiapine and olanzapine are not licensed. Atomoxetine or methylphenidate would be
appropriate if he had ADHD but he does not have this diagnosis. (Ref: Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders in children and young
people: recognition and management. Clinical guideline [CG158] Recommendations#pharmacological-interventions-2).

questions.question_text:
During your CAMHS rotation you become interested in strategies to prevent depression in school age young people. You decide to join a
local project which is o�ering group training on coping strategies and mindfulness to all year 9 students, with additional 1:1 support for
those who are identi�ed to have risk factors for depression. This is an example which of the following types of prevention?
questions.explanation:
This intervention targets all students (universal) and then students who are deemed to be at higher risk for developing depression
(selective). Universal interventions target the general public or a whole population group. Selective interventions focus on a particular group
or subgroup who have biological, psychological or social risk factors for developing a mental disorder. Indicated prevention targets high-risk
individuals with detectable symptoms but whom do not yet meet the criteria for the disorder. (Ref: Weissberg RP, Kumpfer KL, Seligman ME.
Prevention that works for children and youth: An introduction. American Psychological Association; 2003 Jun).

questions.question_text:
Alan Davies is a 11-year-old who has just been diagnosed with ADHD and Tourette's in a local CAMHS clinic. Which of the following drugs
should be prescribed for him in the �rst instance?
questions.explanation:
It is generally recommended that alpha 2 adrenergic agonists, such as Clonidine, are used �rst-line in patients with ADHD and Tourette's.
There is some evidence that stimulants, such as Methylphenidate, can increase the frequency and severity of tics. However, further evidence
suggests that Methylphenidate can be well-tolerated in many patients, although Dexamphetamine is thought to signi�cantly worsen tics and
should be avoided.

questions.question_text:
Matthew Twist is a 17-year-old boy with a diagnosis of conduct disorder. He attends your clinic with his mother but just before you call them
in, she asks to speak to you in private for a few moments. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Insist that she speaks in front of her son
Ask another member of sta� to sit in on the consultation
Speak to the mother and then continue with the consultation
Deny the request and continue with the consultation
Ask permission of the boy and speak to the mother if permitted

correct_answer.text: Ask permission of the boy and speak to the mother if permitted

questions.explanation:
Children older than 16 years of age can generally be assumed to have capacity to make decisions about their treatment and care and should
be consulted regarding these matters. However, until they are 18 years, their parents can still consent on their behalf, although resolving
situations like this may involve the courts. Realistically, most 16 and 17 year olds will consent to such a request.

questions.question_text:
Tommy is 7 years old. His mother describes that life at home with him is very challenging: he is frequently not paying attention to her, he
moves around the house very quickly, knocking things over, barging into her room without knocking. His teacher reports that at school he
frequently interrupts her, cannot sit still in his chair and is so distracted he rarely manages to �nish a piece of work. You consider starting
him on medication for ADHD, but in taking a history you also discover he has an autoimmune liver disorder. Which of the following drugs is
contraindicated in patients with ADHD and liver disease?
questions.explanation:
Atomoxetine is extensively metabolised in the liver by cytochrome P450 and associated with liver injury; its use is therefore contraindicated
in patients with liver disease.

questions.question_text:
You are working with a family in which one of the children has experienced sexual abuse. Which disorder is she most likely to develop in
adulthood?
questions.explanation:
Personality Disorder is the adulthood diagnostic grouping with the highest relative risk in children who have experienced childhood sexual
abuse. (BJPsych 2004, 184:416-421)

questions.question_text:
Stella is a 15-year-old girl who has been losing weight over the preceding 9 months. Her mother reports that she counts the number of
calories in her food, avoids eating with the rest of the family, and has taken to running several kilometres every day. What are the most
important features of an initial assessment in clinic?
questions.explanation:
Measurement of weight and height, so as to work out the BMI, is crucial in the initially assessment as it will help to steer the direction of
subsequent consultations, investigations and interventions. A BMI below 17.5 is a feature of anorexia nervosa.

questions.question_text:
Natasha is a 19-year-old woman with a BMI of 15.8; she has been restricting her food intake for the past six months. She exercises daily in
an e�ort to lose more weight. She believes she is overweight, despite evidence to the contrary. She does not wish to engage in talking
therapy. You consider starting her on medication. Which of these would be the best initial option?
questions.explanation:
Pharmacological medication is not indicated as the sole treatment of anorexia nervosa. It may be used to treat co-morbid mental illness,
such as depression, once the patient's weight has stabilised. Meta-analyses in the use of antipsychotics have failed to show e�cacy for body
weight and other anorexia-related outcomes (J Clin Psychiatry 2012; 73(6):e757-66).

questions.question_text:
Mr O'Mahony has had Parkinson's disease for 2 years and has now been diagnosed with Parkinson's dementia. He has recently started
experiencing distressing visual hallucinations after having seen his neurologist last week. What would be the �rst line management strategy
for new psychotic symptoms in someone with Parkinson's dementia?

options.text: Review Parkinson's medications and consider reducing in consultation with neurologist

correct_answer.text: Review Parkinson's medications and consider reducing in consultation with neurologist

questions.explanation:
The NICE guidelines for Parkinson's disease state that the �rst course of action in new hallucinations is to reduce the dosage of any
Parkinson's disease medicines that might have triggered hallucinations or delusions, taking into account the severity of symptoms and
possible withdrawal e�ects. Seek advice from a healthcare professional with specialist expertise in Parkinson's disease before modifying
therapy. Haloperidol is contraindicated in Parkinson's disease for its potential to worsen Parkinsonism and cause life threatening extra
pyramidal side e�ects. Lithium is not indicated. Quetiapine may be considered if the symptoms are distressing and do not respond to other
treatments. However, if Mr O'Mahony is not yet on a cholinesterase inhibitor this would the best medication to start prior to adding
antipsychotics. (Ref: Parkinson's disease in adults. NICE guideline [NG71] Published date: July
2017.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Brenda Yung is a 82 year old woman with a diagnosis of mild Alzheimer' disease who wishes to remain in her home as long as possible.
Her family is keen for her to move to a residential home. They are querying her capacity to make a decision around this. Which of the
following is not true regarding mental capacity?

options.text: It applies to general decisions about every day issues
It can only be assessed by a psychiatrist
It can be enhanced by repeated discussions
It can vary and be present at sometimes and not at others
It may be impaired for one decision but not another

correct_answer.text: It can only be assessed by a psychiatrist

questions.explanation:
Mental capacity does not have to be assessed by a psychiatrist. A wide variety of healthcare and legal professionals should be able to assess
capacity, particularly with reference to their speci�c professional roles. Psychiatrists can be asked to assist if the decision is di�cult or
contentious.

questions.question_text:
Dillan is 6 years old. His parents report that he has been found to have moderate learning di�culties. He is rather socially anxious, makes
poor eye contact, is prone to losing his temper quite easily. On examination he has large ears and a long face. What is the most likely genetic
disorder?
questions.explanation: Fragile X occurs in both genders but is more common in males than females; the FMR1 Gene is implicated, located on the X chromosome.

questions.question_text:
Mark and Jenny's 26-month old daughter has been observed to lose many of the motor and verbal skills she had previously developed. For
example, she is now unable to walk, her hands are making repeated movements seemingly without purpose, she no longer uses sentences
in her speech. She has also begun to have seizures. Which of the following condition is this clinical picture highly suggestive of?
questions.explanation:
Retts Syndrome is a rare, non-inherited genetic postnatal neurological disorder that occurs almost exclusively in girls resulting in severe
mental and physical disability, including due to seizures.

questions.question_text:
Eva has a diagnosis of high functioning autism. She has a particular fascination with patterns in music and is able to perceive and describe
complex reoccurring patterns. What description can be given to this particular talent?
questions.explanation:
Systematizing is the drive to analyse or construct systems and recognising repeating patterns in stimuli. This is a common feature of those
with autistic spectrum disorders (see Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci 2009; 364 (1522): 1377-1383)

questions.question_text:
Mr David McDermott is a 40-year-old man with a diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome. He has recently been referred to his local psychiatric
clinic due to concerns about his mental health. Which of the following psychiatric disorders is most strongly associated with DiGeorge
syndrome?
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia is most strongly associated, with up to 30% of those with DiGeorge syndrome developing a psychotic illness.

questions.question_text:
In your CAMHS clinic you are seeing Skye, a 3-year-old child with developmental delay. Her mother reports she had hypocalcaemia soon
after she was born. Which ONE of the following syndromes are associated with neonatal hypocalcaemia?
questions.explanation:
In DiGeorge syndrome neonatal hypocalcaemia can result from hypoparathyroidism secondary to parathyroid aplasia or hypoplasia. The
other disorders listed are not associated with neonatal hypocalcaemia. (References: Carpenter et al, 2017. Etiology of neonatal
hypocalcaemia.
